title: Tkhines: Prayer in Yiddish
hookLine: Sarah Rebecca Rachel Leah Horowitz, an eighteenth-century scholar, wrote a tkhine in Hebrew, Aramaic and Yiddish
carry: the mishnah lets the heart pray in any language
tomorrow: the last night of something. why does a sad song help?

lines: A VOICE NOTE, HALF AND HALF.
cards: A voice note from a grandmother: half in English, half in the language she grew up with, and one word in the middle she never translates because it doesn't need translating.
You can hear the kitchen in it, and the stove, and the radio she always leaves on. Some words only sound right in the language you first heard them in.
For generations of Jewish women in Eastern Europe, Hebrew was the language of the prayer book, and Yiddish was the language of the kitchen, the market and the heart.
So what did a grandmother pray in, if Hebrew wasn't hers?

teach.b: She prayed in tkhines. A tkhine is a personal prayer, usually in Yiddish, often written for women: for lighting candles, for baking bread, for a child who is sick, for a husband on the road.
They sound like someone talking, because they were meant to be said by someone talking. One tkhine stands out.
Sarah Rebecca Rachel Leah Horowitz, a learned woman, wrote hers in three languages: Hebrew, Aramaic and Yiddish. She knew the scholars' tongues, and she chose to put the everyday one beside them.
The tkhine was not a lesser prayer for people who couldn't manage Hebrew.
It was a door for prayer in the language you dream in. And here's the fact to tell a friend tonight: the Mishnah already said it.
In Sotah, it lists the Shema, the central prayer and the grace after meals among the words that may be said in any language. The rabbis wanted the heart to understand what the mouth was saying.
There is an older teacher behind all this too.

In the book of Samuel, Hannah prays for a child with only her lips moving, no sound at all. The Talmud learns from her how to pray: quietly, meaning every word. A whisper in your own words, said with your whole self.

how: Collections of tkhines were printed for Jewish women in Yiddish, with prayers for candle-lighting, baking challah, pregnancy and sickness; today some Jews pray core prayers in English or another language, as the Mishnah allows.

s: Jewish prayer only counts if it's said in Hebrew
the Mishnah (Sotah 7:1) lists the Shema, prayer and the grace after meals as words that may be said in any language.
tkhines were personal prayers for everyday moments like baking bread
candles, bread, a sick child, a husband on the road: they sound like someone talking.
tkhines were for people who couldn't learn Hebrew
Horowitz knew Hebrew and Aramaic and still wrote in Yiddish beside them. it was a door, not a lesser prayer.

games.q: your grandfather wants to say Kaddish for his brother, but his Hebrew has faded and he's embarrassed. what do today's sources suggest?
o: he can mean every word in the language he lives in; the Mishnah allows many prayers that way.
he should stay silent until his Hebrew comes back, since only Hebrew is real prayer.
he should hand the whole thing to someone else, since meaning it isn't the point.
games.why: the Mishnah lets the Shema, prayer and grace be said in any language, and the tkhines show prayer in the language of the heart. (Kaddish itself is mostly Aramaic; some read it from a transliteration with a translation beside it.)

practice: Listen for the sound of your first language, the one you think in when you're tired. Say one line out loud in it, quietly, the way Hannah's lips moved: if you pray, a line to God; if not, one thing you're grateful for.
Then say it once more, slower, and let the sound of it be the whole sit.

wordCard.voice: Women's words: the tkhines, prayers in Yiddish and beside it Hebrew and Aramaic. Prayer in the language you live in.

orig.note: Hebrew: a plea, a supplication. In Yiddish, tkhine (TKHI-neh).

carryVoice: Your line: the Mishnah lets the heart pray in any language. The tkhines did it in Yiddish. That's today.
